items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1363

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the real property actions and proceedings law, in
relation to foreclosure notices


 PURPOSE :

Provides special protections to tenants of properties that have been
foreclosed

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Adds a new subdivision 6 to section 1303 of the real property actions
and proceedings law requiring tenants to be notified when the
ownership of the subject property changes ownership due to a
foreclosure proceeding. Additionally, if the new owner wishes to evict
the current tenants of the subject property within 6 months of taking
ownership, such owner shall be required to give tenants 30 days notice
of their intent to commence eviction proceedings.

 JUSTIFICATION :

While New York policymakers have been focusing on finding ways to
assist homeowners stay in their homes and asking financial
institutions to work with families to assist in that request, the
plight of renters living in foreclosed properties has been largely
forgotten.  Many properties facing foreclosure in New York --
including single-family homes and multifamily buildings -- are
investment properties occupied by these renters, leaving thousands of
families at risk of eviction. More importantly, these evictions
proceed against renters who have paid their rent on a timely and
regular basis.

When a landlord becomes in default on their mortgage they are notified
after a certain period of time that a foreclosure action has been
started against them in court. They can either choose to negotiate
with the lender on an acceptable payment plan or if so needed they can
discuss a modification of the mortgage to make the loan more afford.
If the landlord does not become current on the mortgage, the
foreclosure process will continue and the home will eventually be put
up for auction. When this home is put up for auction it can either be
purchased by an individual, another banking or lending institution, or
it can remain the property of the foreclosing lending institution and
become which is referred to as an REO property. Whatever the case may
be, the foreclosing bank will then file an eviction notice against the
landlord to clear the property. Unfortunately more often than not the
landlord is not the sole occupant of the property. In fact many times
the property is not owner-occupied and what results is scores of
tenants not realizing they have lost their shelter until there is a
Marshall's notice on the door letting them know they have to move
because the house has been sold.

On HousingPolicy.org, a project of the Center for Housing Policy, the
impact of this issue has been discussed and studied by various
non-profits.

* A 2008 study of rental housing in the United States which notes that
almost 20 percent of all foreclosures are rental properties.
* Another 2008 study indicates that rental properties could be
involved in 38 percent of foreclosures nationally and approximately
half of foreclosures in Nevada, Illinois, and New York.


This legislation would provide notice to affected tenants of a
foreclosure and of any plans to terminate their tenancy through
eviction.

* Within 30 days of taking ownership of a foreclosed property, bank or
new owner shall provide written notice of the change in ownership to
tenants and occupants by certified mail with a signed receipt. Until
this notice is served, tenants shall not be liable for paying rent to
the bank or new owner.
* Bank or new owner must file proof of service of notice of its
ownership at the commencement of any proceeding to collect rent from a
tenant or occupant of a foreclosed property.
* Bank or new owner shall provide written notice of any intent to
evict a tenant or occupant by certified mail with a signed receipt at
least 30 days prior to the commencement of an eviction proceeding.
* Bank or new owner must file proof of service of notice of its intent
to evict at the commencement of any proceeding to evict a tenant or
occupant of a foreclosed property.
* This section shall only apply where the tenant or occupant is not
the mortgagor or a member of the mortgagor's household and the lease
or tenancy is the result of an arms-length transaction.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

None. This is new legislation.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the 90th day after it shall have become
a law and shall apply to any foreclosure proceeding that takes place
on or after such date regardless if such proceeding was commenced
prior to such date.

C.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S1363C

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the civil practice law and rules and the real property
actions and proceedings law, in relation to evictions of tenants upon
foreclosure of a property


 PURPOSE :

Provides special protections to tenants of properties that have been
foreclosed.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

1. Amends section 5102 of the CPLR to afford tenants in residential
buildings with fewer than 6 dwelling units 90 days notice prior to an
execution directing delivery of the premises if that property has been
foreclosed in the prior 6 months.
2. Amends section 221 of the RPAPL to afford tenants in residential
buildings with fewer than 6 dwelling units 90 days notice prior to an
execution directing delivery of the premises if that property has been
foreclosed in the prior 6 months.
3. Amends section 713 of the RPAPL to afford tenants in residential
buildings with fewer than 6 dwelling units 90 days notice prior to
commencement of a special proceeding to obtain possession the premises
if that property has been foreclosed in the prior 6 months.
4. Amends section 1301 of the RPAPL to require foreclosure summonses
to contain notices to tenants of residential buildings with fewer than
6 dwelling units.
5. Amends section 1303 of the RPAPL to give tenants in residential
buildings with fewer than 6 dwellings units notice similar to the
notice already given to homeowners in foreclosure of the availability
of housing counseling services.
6. Amends section 1305 of the RPAPL to require notice to tenants in
residential buildings with fewer than 6 dwelling units of the
commencement of a foreclosure action, the result of that action and
any resulting change in building ownership. New-tenants must also be
given notice of the pendency and status of a foreclosure action at the
time they sign a lease.
7. If notice of a change of building ownership is not given within 30
days to tenants in a residential building with fewer than 6 dwelling
units, such tenants are relieved of their obligation to pay rent until
such notice is given.
8. Amends section 1311 of the RPAPL to provide that foreclosing
entities must make good faith efforts to ascertain the identity of any
tenants residing in a covered building before serving them notice of a
foreclosure as 'john or jane doe" 9. Amends sections 1311 and 1351 of
the RPAPL to provide that tenancy of tenants not named in a
foreclosure action is not affected by the judgment in that action.

 JUSTIFICATION :

While New York policymakers have been focusing on finding ways to
assist homeowners stay in their homes and asking financial
institutions to work with families to assist in that request, the
plight of renters living in foreclosed properties has been largely
forgotten.  Many properties facing foreclosure in New York --
including single-family homes and multifamily buildings -- are

families at risk of eviction. More importantly, these evictions
proceed against renters who have paid their rent on a timely and
regular basis.

after a certain period of time that a foreclosure action has been
started against them in court. They can either choose to negotiate
with the lender on an acceptable payment plan or if so needed they can
discuss a modification of the mortgage to make the loan more afford.
If the landlord does not become current on the mortgage, the
foreclosure process will continue and the home will eventually be put
up for auction. When this home is put up for auction it can either be
purchased by an individual, another banking or lending institution, or
it can remain the property of the foreclosing lending institution and
become which is referred to as an REO property. Whatever the case may
be, the foreclosing bank will then file an eviction notice against the
landlord to clear the property. Unfortunately more often than not the
landlord is not the sole occupant of the property. In fact many times
the property is not owner-occupied and what results is scores of
tenants not realizing they have lost their shelter until there is a
Marshal's notice on the door letting them know they have to move
because the house has been sold.

On HousingPolicy.org, a project of the Center for Housing Policy, the
impact of this issue has been discussed and studied by various
non-profits.

* A 2008 study of rental housing in the United States which notes that
almost 20 percent of all foreclosures are rental properties.
* Another 2008 study indicates that rental properties could be
involved in 38 percent of foreclosures nationally and approximately
half of foreclosures in Nevada, Illinois, and New York.

This legislation would provide notice to affected tenants of a
foreclosure and of any plans to recover possession of the property, as
well as an additional 90 days notice before any applicable proceeding
is commenced.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
None. This is new legislation.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the 90th day after it shall have become
a law.

summary: Provides special protections to tenants of properties that have been foreclosed.
